p: I do.
Thank you. You can begin when ready.

Thank you so much. Good afternoon, Chair Thomas-Henry, Chair Feliz, Members of the City Council's Committee on Small Business and Public Safety. My name is Haris Khan, and I serve as Chief of Staff at the New York City Department of Small Business Services. I'm pleased to join today's hearing with Deputy Chief of Patrol Services Thomas Alps from the New York City Police Department. At SBS, we deliver economic security for all New Yorkers by connecting them to good jobs,

supporting small businesses, and investing in our neighborhoods. New York City's more than 180,000 small businesses are the backbone of our economy. From COVID-19 to the blizzard conditions last weekend, our small businesses keep the city running and ensure essential goods and services reach those in need. Our city thrives when small businesses thrive and, as such, we take incidents of retail theft very seriously. Repeat retail thefts can deteriorate the stability of a mom-and-pop store, the livability of our commercial corridors, and can drive workers and customers away from small businesses. We're encouraged and grateful for our partners in law enforcement as we see retail theft incidents trending downwards year over year. In responding to the post-pandemic rise in retail theft, local District Attorney's offices and NYPD have adapted their efforts and deployed new strategies to successfully reduce retail theft. These strategies include trainings to businesses on how they can issue trespass notices and new ways to tackle organized retail theft. Since 2025, retail theft has declined by 14 percent citywide. SBS has also promoted the

City's voluntary Small Business Security Camera Integration Program to expedite investigations. This program provides NYPD real-time access to cameras in participating small businesses and first began as a pilot in the Flushing Business Improvement District in 2023 before a citywide expansion in 2024. A primary way that SBS boosts neighborhood resiliency and supports public safety is through our close work with the New York City's network of 78 Business Improvement Districts, also known as BIDs. SBS oversees and partners with the citywide BID network that invests more than 207 million in neighborhoods annually, covers more than 300 miles of commercial corridors, and serves 25,000 storefront businesses. In FY25, BIDs spent 32 million dollars, roughly 15 percent of total spending, on public safety measures, and roughly half of all BIDs deliver enhancements such as pedestrian security cameras and public safety ambassadors. At SBS, we fund many of these efforts through our small BID support grants, which further impact and build capacity for smaller organizations. Over the last two fiscal years, we've also helped small businesses

secure over 120 million dollars in financing assistance to cover a variety of expenses. We provide one-on-one appointments with trained staff through our seven Business Solution Centers who help businesses review financial products, clarify eligibility rules, and identify required documentation. Small businesses can get connected to our services and lending partners in person at our centers, but also online through our NYC Funds Finder platform, which is the first-of-its-kind digital marketplace for small business loans and grants. We also connect businesses to our Business Preparedness and Resiliency Program, also known as BPREP, and as part of this program, businesses can receive a free on-site risk assessment to identify vulnerabilities and boost overall resiliency. Eligible businesses can also receive grants of up to 5,000 dollars to shore up their infrastructure with items like generator, fire and flood-proof storage, flood barriers, hardware drives for critical data, and security cameras. And lastly, SBS also promotes New York State's 5-million-dollar commercial security tax credit program that Governor Hochul announced in

January 2024. This State incentive can cover expenses such as security guards, surveillance cameras for small businesses, panic and alarm systems, access control systems, locks, gates, and other structural reinforcement. We shared guidance with community boards, partners, partner organizations, BIDs, elected official offices, and our merchant association partners in advance of last year's October application deadline for that State 5-million-dollar tax credit program. And we also greatly appreciate that Governor Hochul's proposed in her January Executive Budget presentation, the State has proposed an extension of that State tax credit for another three fiscal years. I'd like to now turn to the bills being heard today. Intro. 553 sponsored by Chair Feliz would require SBS or another agency designated by the Mayor to establish a financial assistance program for small businesses purchasing security system technology. Intro. 623 sponsored by Council Member Louis would require SBS in consultation with NYPD to create a year-long pilot program to install security measures for businesses in zip codes with high rates

of retail theft. SBS supports any efforts that help small businesses tackle retail theft, and we appreciate the City Council's attention to these matters. On the proposed legislative package, we recommend an assessment of current City and State efforts to inform the proposed new programming. Between the changes in law enforcement practices, the availability of the State's tax credit program, and the meaningful downward trend in retail theft, we believe current efforts are also leading to an on-the-ground improvement. We look forward to continuing our partnership with Members of the City Council to advance shared prosperity for all New Yorkers, and thank you again for the opportunity to testify today. I look forward to your questions.

Good afternoon, Chair Thomas-Henry and Chair Feliz and Council Members. My name is Thomas Alps. I'm the Executive Officer of the Patrol Services Bureau for the New York City Police Department. On behalf of the Police Commissioner, Jessica Tisch, I thank you for the opportunity to speak with you today about retail theft.

The mission of the New York City Police Department is to protect the lives of property and all who live, work, and visit our city, and to maintain conditions in which our city's small businesses and commercial retailers can thrive. Retail theft poses a direct threat to this mission. Retail theft is a recidivist-driven crime that spiked in the early 2020s, the impact of which was felt across the city by local businesses and the communities they serve. Under Commissioner Tisch, the Department developed and implemented a new policing strategy to target and respond to increases in crime, including retail theft. The NYPD utilized real-time crime statistics to identify patterns driving retail theft, allowing us to respond with focus and urgency. The Department launched new holiday zones to deploy over 200 officers to high-propensity retail corridors during peak hours, and the Department shifted from pass-through enforcement to sustained investigations. The results speak for themselves. Retail theft declined by 14 percent citywide in 2025, and nearly half of all retail theft complaints resulted in an arrest, which was the highest rate since 2019. In our

holiday zones, retail theft declined by 35.7 percent during deployment hours compared to last year. Year-to-date, there has been a 22.5 percent decrease in reported retail theft incidents compared to the same time frame last year. This continued downward trend further demonstrates that data-driven strategic deployment and precision policing produces measurable results. The Department is also proud to partner directly with retailers and small business associations. Through crime prevention seminars, precinct community councils, and direct outreach, we provide best practice guidance on surveillance placement, inventory control practices, and incident reporting protocols. While enforcement remains a critical component to reducing crime, meaningfully reducing retail theft requires continued collaboration between retailers, the community, and the NYPD. Finally, regarding the bills being heard today, Intro. 623 requires the Commissioner of Small Business Services to create a small business security measures pilot program in consultation with the

Police Commissioner. The pilot program would be limited to New York City zip codes with high rates of crimes associated with retail theft, which would be determined by the Police Commissioner. The Department supports the goals of this legislation, and we look forward to working with the Council to craft a version of this legislation that most effectively achieves those goals. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today, and I look forward to answering your questions.

Okay. Thank you both for your testimony. I have a couple of questions, and then we'll turn it over to Chair Feliz and my other Colleagues for questions. First, both of you mentioned a decline in retail theft. What data does SBS rely on to analyze retail theft trends? And within that, do you take into account businesses that may have closed and/or businesses that are no longer reporting?
Thank you, Chair. We're relying on COMPStat and the retail theft data that the NYPD has, so I'll defer to Chief Thomas.

Thank you, Chair. So, I'll speak retail theft data overall from the Police Department. So, retail theft peaked in 2022 with 63,754 retail theft-related crimes. That's robberies that began as a shoplifting incident, grand larcenies, and petit larcenies. Retail theft over the past three years, 2023, declined 7.2 percent, or 4,572 fewer retail theft complaints; in 2024, we had a slight uptick, 3.7 percent increase, or 2,197 additional complaints in that year; 2025, we saw a drastic decrease in retail theft complaints, 14.1 percent decrease, or 8,645 fewer retail theft complaints; 2026, we're building on those successes, we're down 18.8 percent, or 1,507 less retail theft complaints. A lot of our strategy is built across multiple bureaus within the Police Department. We have eight different bureaus working on our efforts to combat retail theft, beginning first and foremost with our Chief of Crime Control Strategies Bureau. They're our analytical arm. They're analyzing the

crimes. They're analyzing those who are actually committing the crimes. They're implementing plans, drafting plans, and they're creating the strategy. Patrol Services Bureau, which I fall under, executes the strategy. We make sure that the deployment is proper. The response times are at its minimal times. We want to get to these incidents as quick as possible. There's a lot of oversight, and there's also a lot of communication with our local District Attorney's office. Both the Chief of Crime Control Strategies and the Patrol Services Bureau are in constant collaboration with the DAs regarding what we're seeing, our trends, our crimes, who we're arresting, and we're talking prosecutorial strategies or diversion programs. Following that, we have our Crime Prevention Officers who are officers in our local commands or are communicating with our BIDs and also partnering with the BIDs and communicating and partnering with all the businesses within the command. They're given best practices about timely reporting, the importance of gathering details when an incident occurs, how to document it internally,

how to use de-escalation techniques, their role in prosecution, the availability of video. We do site surveys and positioning of merchandise. We give them best practices, and then, in addition, we help formulate a communication band where they communicate with each other, and we're part of that. For instance, I can speak specifically up into the Bronx on Fordham Road, how we implemented something like that. Then we have our Detective Bureau that follows up on any complaints where we don't make a summary arrest. We have our detectives on the back end investigating all these crimes. These aren't crimes that we shy away from. We investigate it fully. In full transparency, we now have retail theft on our COMPStat pages, so normally a COMPStat page would show seven major crimes, the most serious crimes. Retail theft is amongst them, so we're showing the importance of combating retail theft, that we are tracking it, and we're sharing that with the public. Our Detective Bureau is investigating these crimes, pulling video in hopes of resolving them successfully, however that may look to arrest. We have Grand Larceny Divisions within the Detective

Bureau that are looking at patterns and trends and organized groups. We have our Intelligence Bureau that's looking at our recidivists, who are these people that are committing these crimes over and over. We put in tracking methods, and then the last bureau would be the Legal Bureau, who is also coordinating with the DAs in the prosecution. We do have a lot of successes to speak of that are significant. I spoke earlier about the holiday zones that was implemented by the Chief of Crime Control Strategies to combat retail theft. It began in November 24th, 2025. (TIMER CHIME)
But in that data, though, it sounds like you guys aren't currently accounting for any businesses that closed down and are not reporting?
I don't have any specific data as it relates to that.
Okay. You had talked about repeat offenders. Is there any data that talks about large-scale theft rings that are stealing to resell versus those who are stealing out of need and necessity?

When we talk about organized theft, the NYPD loosely defines that as two or more persons acting in concert to commit a larceny and several incidents within that. Our Grand Larceny Divisions and our Theft Task Force would be involved in investigating them. In 2025, we had 39 grand larceny patterns involving two or more persons committing theft from retail stores. Currently in 2026, we have eight patterns involving two or more persons involved in retail theft. All the ones in 2025 are closed except for two to arrest, and in 2026, four remain open of the eight. Normally, we're seeing mostly it's individual theft driving this, not organized groups. We do have open patterns in Manhattan, Queens, and Staten Island that involve Lululemon, Aloe, and Target, where large groups are coming in and stealing merchandise en masse. Those are currently under investigation.

You mentioned the DAs and the coordination with the DAs. From my understanding, each of the different District Attorney's offices have their own different programs to combat retail theft. Do you have an opinion in

terms of which have worked the best or have proven the best results or decreased recidivism?

I would say that from the highest levels in the Police Department, from Chief of Crime Patrol Strategies all the way down to local commanders to even borough commanders, we're in constant communication with the DA's office, whether it's their General Crimes Bureau or their Crime Strategy Unit. These are dedicated District Attorneys that are focused on these type of crimes. They make the assessment after reviewing the individual, what's driving this crime, why did he commit this crime, and they make that assessment at the DA's level. We provide information on that individual that we can, but our approach is bringing it to the District Attorney's office. We give them the data that they need to make those assessments, and also to prosecute, whether it's video evidence or such, and they make that decision whether it's going to go towards a diversion program or we're going to go through a prosecutorial criminal conviction.

I want to acknowledge that we have been joined by a Council Member Nurse. I'm going to ask one more question and turn it over to my Colleagues. The United Bodega Association and Economic Development Corporation were partnered to administer the Silent Shields Initiative that gave bodegas panic buttons. How many businesses received these buttons, and did SBS provide any advice or support to create this initiative or administer it?

Thank you, Chair. This program was created by the Economic Development Corporation, and my understanding is former First Deputy Mayor Mastro to provide bodegas with panic buttons. We've heard from the Economic Development Corporation that 302 bodegas received panic buttons during this fiscal year, and it's a one-year program as far as I understand.
And do you get regular updates?

We've asked for updates ahead of this hearing to understand what

EDC's program has led to, and they've shared that it has led to 302 bodegas benefiting from panic buttons. And it's the United Bodega Association on the ground that's installing these panic buttons.
Got it. Thank you. Chair Feliz.

Thank you. Thank you so much, Co-Chair. So, I represent District 15 in the Bronx. District 15 covers many different vibrant commercial corridors, including Fordham Road, the busiest commercial corridor in the entire borough of the Bronx. And I've obviously had a lot of conversations with different stakeholders and businesses that the local BIDs about, we've had a lot of conversations about this topic. One thing that we all know is that retail theft is a complex issue. There's a lot of people that are committing it due to different needs, also mental health challenges, also substance abuse challenges, but then there also is a category specifically committing it in the way of organized retail theft. And just want to say that retail theft

is not a harmless act. It has real consequences on consumers, but also on workers who have to fear for their safety. These are cases that can and do generally escalate, as we've seen. And it also has an effect on businesses. It can significantly affect their ability to operate and stay open. I mean, just imagine a business consistently getting affected by retail theft. How are they going to have items to sell? How are they going to be able to earn money to be able to keep the gates open and be able to pay their workers and so much more? So, a complex issue that requires a lot of different… that we resolve it and tackle it through different angles, but this is not a harmless act. It has real consequences on consumers, their quality of life, the workers, their safety, and, of course, the small businesses and their ability to stay open. So, I have a few questions. I'll start with SBS, questions for SBS. So, what are initiatives that SBS has worked on related to retail thefts? Earlier you mentioned in your testimony that I think it was 15 million dollars in grants on the issue, if I got the number correctly.

So, Chair Feliz, thank you so much. And it's been great. Your focus on this issue has really, I think, over the years as you've led the Small Business Committee in the last term, we've seen the reduction in retail theft. As the State then launched their tax credit, the City modified their practices with the DA's offices and started deploying new strategies. On retail theft, the number that we shared in testimony on financing, that's the general broad stroke work of our small business support teams that connect with small businesses across the five boroughs. And over the past two years, we had that 150-plus-million dollars in financing. And when we connect folks to financing assistance, the small businesses are generally able to use them for a variety of expenses. They can get it for working capital. They can get it for inventory. They can certainly get it to install security cameras. And generally, the need in the small business community that we hear is for larger amounts of financing to be able to sustain their business, grow their business, and open up new stores and really sustain themselves

amidst an affordability crisis that has also impacted small business owners. So. we do financing for small businesses. We connect them to low-cost, affordable lending partners. And through that work, they've gotten over 150 just over the past two years. Separate from that, when the State announced their Commercial Security Tax Credit, we made sure business owners were aware of this, and we promoted it at the time when the application window was open at the State. It seems to open during the fall, so we try to target our outreach during the fall months right before the deadline so that business owners can quickly sign up for that tax credit.
Any grants available to help small businesses on this issue?

There are no grants available on security cameras itself. There is a Business Preparedness and Resiliency Program that we operate at SBS. The eligibility for that program is really focused on neighborhoods in New York City and businesses that fall under the flood plain of the city, and if they're impacted by coastal flooding and similar infrastructural challenges, they're eligible

for that program. The program first provides a free assessment onsite where businesses can get a sense of their vulnerabilities and ways in which we can boost their resiliency. And if in that assessment we realize they don't have security cameras or cameras could be a useful tool for them, then the grants have been used. Per our data, 35 percent of all of our business preparedness and resiliency grant awardees have leveraged the grant to purchase security-related measures.
What is SBS' position on my bill, Intro. 553, also known as the Small Business Protection Act?

Thank you, Chair. On both bills, we are fully aligned on the goal of tackling retail theft and we are fully supportive of any efforts that could bring further reduction on retail theft or help resolve these issues that business owners are struggling with. It's in the program design that we'd love to work with you and the sponsors to make sure that whatever programming that the City embarks on to further this really strong and significant downward trend that we've

started to realize over the past two years, that the work and the programming that's set up complements existing efforts. So. there's the existing State tax credit. We want to make sure that we fully leverage that State tax credit and we don't create a situation where there's two competing products from two levels of government and business owners that are already confused about all of our acronyms have to now be confused with another set of acronyms. We want to make sure that doesn't happen. And so there are ways in which we can work with the leadership of both Committees, the Members that have sponsored the legislation in development to ensure that we maximize both the tax credit and build upon other resources that could help the business community.

Thank you. And now some questions for the NYPD, and I'll be brief. I know we have a pretty big bench, so I'll ask some questions and then I'll pass it on to Colleagues. So, let's start with data related to retail theft. Can you provide a breakdown of retail theft-related complaints that were received, broken down by, let's say, the past four years?
Say that again?
So, retail theft complaints in the City of New York that you received, data for the past four years, broken down year by year.

Broken down year by year. So, 2023, we had 59,131 retail-related complaints versus in 2022, we had 63,703. That was a 7.2 percent decline. 2024, we had 61,328 retail theft complaints versus 59,131 in 2023. 2025… excuse me?
Oh, sorry. Go ahead.

2025, we had 52,683 retail theft-related complaints versus the 61,328 in 2024. And currently, where we stand year-to-date, we're at 6,500 versus 8,007 in 2025. So, we're seeing it trend downward. You know, retail theft peaked in 2022 with 63,754 complaints. And you move over, and we spoke about recidivism and repeat offenders. We made 28,082 shoplifting arrests in 2025. 18,154, or 64.6 percent, have a prior shoplifting arrest. In 2021, and I use that because that was like the high watermark, we peaked with 74.9 percent of our arrests

had a prior shoplifting arrest. So, recidivism from 2021 has dropped from 74.9 percent to 64.6 percent. So, we're seeing that recidivism rate decline, which is a great sign. Very optimistic about that. And it's the efforts of the DAs as well as the NYPD and being more strategic where we're deploying in the retail areas during our most critical times, especially during the holiday months, and we're putting officers that are in administrative duties, newer officers on foot in business districts to protect these businesses, and we're doing it strategically based on data that we're seeing.
Can you provide data on retail theft complaints? I guess any pre-COVID numbers, 2020, 2021, 2019?
I don't have that in front of me. I would have to get back to you on that.
Would you say, so you mentioned we generally, from 2022, '23, '24, '25, generally 59,000 to 63,000 complaints per year, generally more or less?
Yeah. We ranged from 63,000 in 2022, and we dropped to 52,000 in 2025.
Would you say those numbers are much higher compared to the pre-COVID numbers? I know you mentioned you don't have the numbers on you, but based on what you've seen?
I would have to look at where the high-water mark is, but I believe it was 2021 would have been. I don't have that in front of me. I would have to get back to you on that one.

Okay. And, of course, again, retail theft is a complex issue. We have many different reasons for it, including, again, needs, mental health, substance abuse, but also organized theft. Just curious, what percent of theft is due to organized crime versus other reasons such as needs, different needs?

So, the large portion of theft is individuals. It's not organized crime. But like I mentioned previously, in 2025, we had 39 grand larceny patterns involving organized theft where groups of individuals, two or more, came into a retail establishment and committed theft. Currently, in 2026, we're at eight grand larceny patterns. So, we loosely define organized as two or more committing

retail theft on multiple occasions, and we call them patterns. That's how we're defining this.
And based on the conversations that you and your team have had with different stakeholders, what are the top reasons that we usually see that lead to retail theft?

There's a lot of underlying issues with individuals who we're seeing arrested, whether it's drug addiction, mental health. There's a need sometimes. And then there's other individuals who are doing it for profit. Regardless, it's affecting the businesses, and we don't tolerate that, and we look to monitor our arrest rates to make sure we're closing this out and referring them to the District Attorney's office so they can do their assessment. And then we use different strategies, and the DA's office use different strategies to address this. And we really focus mostly on the recidivist offenders. When we talk about our prosecutional strategies, whether that's aggregate charging, where an individual targets the same business multiple times under a short period of time, and that would be the merchandise that is stolen would be added up, and

it would become a grand larceny felony charge. So, that is a prosecutional strategy. Another strategy is the use of trespass affidavits.
Sorry to interrupt. They're having a hard time hearing you online. Can you speak into the mic, please?

The other strategy is trespass affidavits. So, trespass affidavits involve when an individual is arrested, he's served a notice that he's not to enter the establishment again. He gets caught in there, or he or she gets caught in there again, they can be charged with a burglary in a third degree, and that's another way of upgrading enforcement or charges. And the reasoning behind that is we're trying to prevent recidivism, and that's really our focus, and that's the DA's focus, and we're in collaboration and always speaking about that. And the other way is when owners or employees are assaulted or threatened, we use order of protections to protect those employees. So, that's another way to safeguard the employees and the businesses. So, these are prosecutional strategies

that are used to prevent this recidivism and violence towards store owners and businesses.

All right. Two more questions, and then I'll pause. So, what factors does the NYPD think led to the post-2020 spike in retail theft, and also what are programs that NYPD has implemented to help reduce and put an end to retail theft?

So, I can't specifically give you numbers or data as far as who is doing this broken down like that, but we definitely see individuals who have mental health issues that have drug addiction, but we also do see an element that also is driven by profit so we need to address that. Either way, we need to address all of it and however that looks. So, our strategy is simple but very involved. I explained it out. There's many bureaus involved, but it's about sharing intelligence and information with the DAs across the precincts, across the boroughs, because this is a recidivist-driven crime. It's about analyzing it, seeing where our hotspots are, where our corridors or business districts that are most affected, and

deploying officers to prevent, deter, and then make apprehensions should they have, and then it's a relentless follow-up by the detectives should there be no arrest at the initial response. So, that is our approach. It's working. We see the numbers, and we're building on it in 2026. We're doing well.
How many officers have been shifted from administrative duties to the preventing retail theft team?

So, I can speak to that one initiative. Last holiday season, 2025 into 2026, so November 24, 2025, we implemented what we call holiday zones. We analyzed the data. We saw what commands and precincts and areas and business districts were most affected. We deployed 211 officers, administrative in nature, and they were deployed out on foot in these business districts to protect these businesses. So, these were 211 officers each day from November 24th, 2025, to January 12th, 2026. They were deployed there during the businesses when they were open, from 1300 to 2100. They were in Manhattan, Broadway, Union Square, 31st, 34th Street, 42nd Street, 5th Avenue, Madison, St. Nick, in the

Bronx, in the Hub, up on Fordham Road, Broadway. They were on Flatbush and Fulton and Queens. They were on Jamaica and Roosevelt. So, we saw a significant decrease in retail theft in those areas. Specifically, we reduced retail theft by 35.7 percent in those areas that I just spoke of, or 415 less retail theft crimes during that period that I spoke of during those deployment hours. So, it was very analytical and strategic and well thought out and effective.

Earlier you mentioned that retail theft happens for many reasons. A good portion of it is due to substance abuse, mental health, and other challenges. What are programs that the NYPD has worked on together with other agencies to get those individuals the help that they need?

So, we partner with the District Attorney's office. I mean, they're our partners in addressing this issue. A lot of the diversion programs come through them, and we make that assessment when they get introduced to the DA's office. And they're our partners in this, so they're

helping us. Like I said, the recidivism is dropping. I told you the high-water mark, and now it's gone down. So, that's how we address that.
Thank you. Thank you so much. I'll pause for now. Thank you so much. Back to our Co-Chair.

Thank you. I'd like to turn it over to Council Member Cabán for questions. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Thank you. I have quite a few questions. I'm going to ask you to be really succinct, please. I appreciate it. These are about Intro. 623. It requires that the installation of security measures take place in zip codes of New York City with high rates of crime associated with retail theft as determined by the Police Commissioner. So, the first question is what list of crimes are associated with retail theft under that definition?

Right. So, retail theft consists of petite larcenies, simple larcenies under 1,000 dollars from a retail establishment.

Grand larceny would be a theft of over 1,000 dollars. And then it also could include robberies where retail theft occurs, and then they use force to steal that merchandise, and it becomes a robbery. So, those three crimes. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: And burglaries.
Right. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Burg 2s and 3s.

Burg 2s and 3s, correct. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: And the Burg 2 can be either nonviolent or violent. The Burg 3 is inherently nonviolent. So, what constitutes a high rate? Like how will the Commissioner determine the threshold?

Well, I can't speak to that right at this moment. I would have to… COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: I mean, I think that's important information to have, especially when we're talking about this kind of technology. Higher crime rates correspond with zip codes that are already over-policed and over-surveilled. Why should we fund additional surveillance in areas instead of

programs to address the root causes of theft like poverty?

Well, I would say that these businesses, specifically Fordham Road up in the Bronx, a lot of them who partner with us partner voluntarily. A lot of these businesses are employers of the community, and they're struggling, and they need assistance, and we can address this in a… COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: I like that you mentioned that they're struggling because I did a survey of 200 small businesses in my community on public safety and small business. We're really rich with small businesses in Astoria. I know you know that. And actually what they said was while retail theft is a concern and it does happen, their highest priority is their inability to afford rent. That, and then second to that was tariffs and cost of doing business, and then retail theft, and that they end up calling the police because it's really the only area out of those things that give them any sort of relief, but that the fact is that they cannot survive our commercial rent market. So, would you guys be in support of commercial rent stabilization laws?

Thank you, Council Member. I think that's something the Law Department would have to weigh on to see if it's constitutional for the City to establish commercial rent stabilization. But on your point of what you've heard on the ground from community members, 100 percent it's true that what we've heard also is commercial rent continues to be one of the highest costs for businesses, and it's a cost that there's very, very little ability for folks to get relief. We're proud that at the City and at SBS, we've launched a Commercial Lease Assistance Program. It provides pre-litigation support to commercial tenants. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: And I know. I just want to… I appreciate that answer. I just want to move on, but I am glad that what we found in our District is affirmed by the Administration. So, Intro. 623 requires that surveillance footage be capable of… to be viewed through mobile phones, computers, or CCTV. Will anyone who doesn't work for the small business be given access to those feeds?

Council Member, you're referring to the proposed legislation? COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: 623, yeah. It requires that the surveillance footage be capable of being viewed through mobile phones, computers, or CCTV. So, I want to know if anybody that doesn't work for the small business can be given access to those feeds.

I think that's an example on SBS' perspective on the bill. I think that's an area where we would want to have conversations with the Council to make sure that any program that is set up is voluntary, any program that is set up has very strong guardrails. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Can you guarantee that law enforcement won't be given direct access to these feeds?

We're not certain how the final legislation will land in terms of the program design. I wouldn't be able to… kind of as a product of this joint process. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Because contemporaneous access would be a huge problem.

I know that I'm running out of time, so I did want to address some of the testimony that was made. I was a public defender for many years, and I represented well over 1,000 clients, many for different larceny-related offenses. I just want to say that it was stated on the record that the DAs, once an arrest is made and it's passed to them, that their job is that they determine what's driving the theft. That's actually not their mandate or their job. What they are doing is enforcing the law, deciding which things to prioritize, and then some of their metrics include guilty (TIMER CHIME) verdicts, sentences, and those sorts of things. And so, this program of the trespass notice, I just want to lay out for the record what that is legally. I have somebody who I've been on this Council for over four years is still serving an upstate prison sentence for stealing cell phones from a store because he struggled with drug use because of a prior trauma.
